abstract: Communication signals must transmit information efficiently through the physical environment.1,2,3 In subterranean habitats, where visual and airborne acoustic cues are severely constrained,4,5 many animals rely on substrate-borne vibrations.6,7,8 However, it remains unclear whether seismic signals are directed toward intended receivers and whether they encode socially relevant information about the signaler. Here, we investigated seismic communication in the blind mole rat (BMR; Nannospalax galili), a solitary subterranean rodent that produces vibrations by head drumming against tunnel walls.9,10,11 Using a semi-natural outdoor setup equipped with more than 30 geophones, we examined the spatial and informational structure of seismic signaling during social interactions while manipulating the position and sex of conspecific intruders. We found that head-drumming signals were distributed non-uniformly and were biased toward the location of the conspecific intruder, producing a broad directional radiation pattern. Signal production rate was also modulated by social context, as BMRs produced more head drums during opposite-sex than same-sex encounters and exhibited sex-dependent temporal dynamics over the course of interactions. Finally, machine-learning analyses showed that head drumming contains individual-specific structure in both single-drum waveforms and the temporal organization of drum sequences, with individual classification remaining above chance across recording sessions and behavioral roles. Together, these findings establish seismic communication as a receiver-directed, information-rich signaling system that simultaneously encodes spatial, individual, and social information. More broadly, our results extend the principle of receiver-directed communication to the seismic modality and suggest that communication systems can converge on common strategies for transmitting biologically relevant information despite fundamentally different physical environments.

summary: Blind mole rats direct head-drumming seismic signals toward conspecific intruders, with rate varying by sex and encoding individual identity in drum waveforms.
title: Directional seismic signals encode socially relevant information in a solitary rodent.
